prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping allows many neutral atoms to be interrogated at once, bringing optical frequency standards to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I keep B053 as my single public position, and the second round has strengthened rather than weakened my reasons. The chair's first question asks whether we can state in a citation what is new without reaching into ion-clock territory. I think we can: the new element is the magic-wavelength lattice, which removes the light shift on the clock transition so that thousands of neutral atoms are interrogated simultaneously, and the demonstrated consequence is systematic uncertainty near 1e-18 confirmed by independent laboratories. That sentence does not claim the single-ion clock lineage and does not claim the comb. As an instrumentalist I judge this a genuine experimental advance with a measured payoff of two orders of magnitude over the caesium standard, not a refinement. The statutes speak of discovery or invention, and the lattice clock is an invention whose consequences (gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, bounds on drifting constants, the prospective redefinition of the second) are physical results rather than engineering convenience. Every member either prefers B053 or lists it as an alternative, and all eight opening proposals named the same pair, so the attribution is as stable as anything on this shortlist. I am not counting votes in saying this; I am saying that the questions raised against it (metrology versus discovery, overlap with 2005 and 2012) have been answered on the merits by Kroll and Lindroth, and the questions raised against the other candidates (allocation, maturity, overlap) have not been answered by their advocates.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is the one the chair posed: B053 stands on tools honoured in 2005 and 2012, and a committee that wants a new window on nature or a closed fundamental question could reasonably put it behind B046. Eriksson is right that the payoff from a redefined second and from constants tests is still partly prospective, and I should not rest the case on redefinition. The pair also leaves out Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and others, and the supplied credit cannot settle how Katori's proposal weighs against Ye's accuracy programme; the citation should therefore name the architecture and its precision realisation and say no more about priority than that. Finally I note that my reservation about discovery versus invention is shared by supporters of B053 as well as by its critics, and that I have not fully dissolved it; I have judged that it does not outweigh the clean credit and maturity.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B046, the experimental Higgs discovery for Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee, as the unrecognised complement to 2013, accepts that Della Negra is as defensible as Virdee, and says he would not resist B053 if the allocation cannot be made defensible.
responses.response: I agree that the scientific case is overwhelming and that the Higgs observation is unrecognised after 2013; I ranked it third and keep it as my first alternative. You have named the obstacle yourself: choosing three of four founding figures across two experiments cannot be defended as a statement about who made the discovery, since ATLAS and CMS each stand on their own, and replacing Virdee with Della Negra or Jenni with either only moves the arbitrariness. I would not resist B046 if the committee were prepared to accept that cost, but I cannot propose a three-name allocation that I could defend to the Academy, and your own concession that you would accept B053 on that ground is the point on which we converge. I would add that your remark that the Higgs is a closed question and the clock is not a discovery is right as classification, but I do not think classification should outweigh clean credit.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the discovery-versus-invention distinction is not a useful dividing line, that the lattice scheme solves a different problem from ion clocks (many-atom interrogation without a light-shift penalty), and places B009 behind B053 on maturity and attribution.
responses.response: You have moved me on the metrology point. In round 1 I treated discovery versus invention as an open question for the committee; your argument that a factor of one hundred in accuracy opens new measurements, together with the statutory wording, persuades me that it is not a reason to rank the clock lower. I also accept that the ion-clock overlap is real but separable, which is why I now want the citation built on the magic-wavelength lattice. I part from you only on the disclosure: your stay in Hall's laboratory and your field proximity do not disqualify you, but they do mean that Johansson's and Danielsson's more distant assessments are useful checks on the case, and both of them reach the same conclusion. On B009 we now agree in substance, and I have moved it out of my alternatives for the reasons below.

responses.point: Lindroth writes the B053 citation around magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, argues that the statutory emphasis on invention fits, and says she would accept B009 as an alternative but not above B053 while credit among Halzen, Karle and Spiering is unresolved.
responses.response: Your drafting is the best statement of the case I have seen and I have borrowed it: the citation should name magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms and the 1e-18 realisation, and not reach further. I also accept your point that credit among Halzen, Karle and Spiering is unresolved. In round 1 my own configuration for IceCube was Halzen and Spiering only, and Danielsson, Mehlig and Olsson each include Karle; if even I cannot hold my own two-name allocation after reading the others, it is not ready as a prize configuration. That is a candid reversal of my opening first place and I would rather say so than defend it.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B013 for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a durable organising principle that the 2016 prize did not cover, and says the lattice-clock overlap is closer than the 2016 overlap with B013; he lists B053 as his first alternative.
responses.response: Your case that the quantum spin Hall prediction, Z2 classification and HgTe observation fall outside what was honoured in 2016 is the strongest answer to the overlap objection that I have heard, and it is why I now list B013 as an alternative. My difficulty remains the cap: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe structure that Molenkamp measured, and Hasan's three-dimensional work is the other half of the experimental story, so any three names we choose will be read as ranking people within a field of at least six contributors. On overlap I disagree with you in degree: the lattice clock uses cooling and trapping methods honoured earlier, but it is a new scheme, whereas the 2016 prize and B013 share a subject of topological phases. A citation for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp could address the overlap but not the omission, and the omission is why I keep B053 ahead.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B052 for Rose, Haider and Urban as a mature, bounded-group instrumentation advance with no pending interpretive question, and concedes she cannot show it is more transformative than the correlated-electron candidates.
responses.response: I agree that B052 has no maturity question and a coherent trio, and your analogy to the 1986 microscopy prize is fair; I withdraw any suggestion that electron optics is not physics. My remaining reservation is the STEM strand: Krivanek and Dellby are not covered, and you yourself call this unresolved, so the trio is a defensible core but not a complete credit. It is also fair that you disclose your group's use of corrected instruments; I would treat that as a reason to weight your first place with care, not to discount your argument. Between two instrumentation candidates with bounded credit, I find the lattice clock has the broader committee support and the more direct physical consequences (redshift tests, bounds on constants), so I keep it ahead of B052.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a precision-measurement invention as equal in standing to a discovery such as B046, which is the principal point on which the vote may turn.
How the citation can credit the architecture and its precision realisation without understating Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and others outside the two supplied names.
Whether the Higgs allocation (three of Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee and Della Negra) could ever be made defensible; I cannot make it so and I am not certain another member can.
I am relying on recollection of clock uncertainty figures, priorities and roles at the time of announcements, and have not verified these against external sources.
statement.conflict_note: My documented background is in astroparticle instrumentation (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur) and a CERN-based doctorate in experimental particle physics, so I am professionally close to neutrino astronomy (B009) and adjacent to B046; my profile records no specific tie to IceCube, ATLAS or CMS. I have no documented tie to Katori, Ye or any group working on optical lattice clocks and no conflict is apparent for B053. As chair I have tried to treat disclosed proximities of other members (Johansson on B001, Olsson on B052, Eriksson on B033 and B013, Kroll and Lindroth on B053) as information for the committee rather than as grounds to discount any member's argument.
